title: Premchand v. State of Maharashtra
bench: Justice S. Ravindra Bhat and Justice Dipankar Datta
legal_issues: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC,Section 304 Part II IPC,Section 313(5) CrPC Written Statement,Section 307 IPC
procedural_context: Criminal Appeal by Special Leave against Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) dismissal upholding Sessions conviction under S. 302 and S. 307 IPC
actual_holding: Conviction under Section 302 IPC altered to Section 304 Part II IPC and sentenced to period already undergone. Conviction under Section 307 IPC maintained with sentence undergone. Trial Court and High Court committed manifest illegality by failing to consider the written statement filed by the accused under Section 313(5) CrPC.
verbatim_excerpt: The appellant having filed a written statement under sub-section (5) of Section 313 CrPC, the trial Court as well as the High Court committed a manifest illegality in not considering the same... The incident occurred without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel. The ingredients of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC are satisfied. The conviction under Section 302 IPC is altered to Section 304 Part II IPC.

title: Ghapoo Yadav v. State of M.P.
bench: Justice Doraiswamy Raju and Justice Arijit Pasayat
legal_issues: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC,Ingredients of Sudden Fight,Heat of Passion,Section 304 Part II IPC
procedural_context: Appeal against High Court conviction for murder under S. 302 IPC
actual_holding: For Exception 4 to Section 300 to apply, four cumulative conditions must be satisfied: (i) sudden fight; (ii) absence of premeditation; (iii) fight in heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel; and (iv) offender not taking undue advantage or acting in cruel/unusual manner.
verbatim_excerpt: The help of Exception 4 can be invoked if death is caused: (a) without premeditation, (b) in a sudden fight; (c) without the offender having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner; and (d) the fight must have been with the person killed.

title: Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory, Chandigarh
bench: Justice S. Natarajan and Justice A.M. Ahmadi
legal_issues: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC,Sudden Quarrel,Absence of Premeditation,Section 304 Part I IPC
procedural_context: Appeal against murder conviction where sudden altercation over kitchen entry resulted in knife injury
actual_holding: Where a sudden quarrel arose without any prior planning and the accused picked up a knife and inflicted injuries in the heat of passion without taking undue advantage, the offence falls under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. Conviction altered from Section 302 to Section 304.
verbatim_excerpt: To invoke Exception 4 to Section 300, it is not necessary that every blow must be measured. If the accused did not act in a cruel or unusual manner in the sudden fight, conviction under Section 302 cannot stand.

title: Sukhbir Singh v. State of Haryana
bench: Justice R.P. Sethi and Justice K.G. Balakrishnan
legal_issues: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC,Sudden Fight Without Premeditation,Section 304 Part I IPC
procedural_context: Appeal against conviction under S. 302 IPC where altercation occurred over mud splash
actual_holding: The time gap between the sudden quarrel and fight was negligible, showing lack of premeditation. The appellant was entitled to Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC and conviction under Section 302 was altered to Section 304 Part I IPC.
verbatim_excerpt: The time gap between the quarrel and the fight is negligible... The appellant is entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. Conviction altered from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I.

title: Reena Hazarika v. State of Assam
bench: Justice N.V. Ramana, Justice Mohan M. Shantanagoudar, and Justice M.R. Shah
legal_issues: Section 313 CrPC,Defense Explanation,Duty of Court,Failure to Consider Written Explanation
procedural_context: Criminal appeal challenging conviction where lower courts ignored defense explanation under S. 313 CrPC
actual_holding: Section 313 CrPC confers a valuable statutory safeguard. A solemn duty is cast on trial and appellate courts to examine the defense of the accused; omission to consider it causes grave prejudice and vitiates the conviction.
verbatim_excerpt: A solemn duty is cast on the court in dispensing justice to consider the defense of the accused under Section 313 CrPC. An omission to consider the defense causes grave prejudice to the accused.

title: Sanatan Naskar v. State of West Bengal
bench: Justice P. Sathasivam and Justice Swatanter Kumar
legal_issues: Section 313 CrPC,Evidentiary Value of Examination,Judicial Consideration
procedural_context: Appeal concerning evaluation of statements recorded under Section 313 CrPC
actual_holding: Statements of the accused under Section 313 CrPC can be taken into consideration by the court to evaluate the truth or falsity of the prosecution case, though they are not strictly evidence on oath under the Evidence Act.
verbatim_excerpt: The answers given by the accused under Section 313 CrPC may be taken into consideration by the court to test the truth of the prosecution case and the veracity of the defense.

title: Pulicherla Nagaraju @ Nagaraja Reddy v. State of A.P.
bench: Justice B.P. Singh and Justice R.V. Raveendran
legal_issues: Section 302 IPC vs Section 304 Part II IPC,Intention to Cause Death,Determinative Tests
procedural_context: Appeal determining whether single blow to neck/head constituted murder under S. 302 or S. 304 Part II
actual_holding: Court must determine intention from nature of weapon, whether weapon was carried or picked up on the spot, whether blow was aimed at vital part, force used, prior enmity, and whether act was in sudden fight.
verbatim_excerpt: The intention to cause death or cause bodily injury likely to cause death is to be gathered from factors such as nature of weapon, whether it was carried beforehand, part of body struck, and whether there was premeditation.

title: State of Rajasthan v. Shiv Charan
bench: Justice K.S. Radhakrishnan and Justice Dipak Misra
legal_issues: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC,Cruel and Unusual Manner,Undue Advantage Test
procedural_context: State appeal against reduction of murder conviction to Section 304
actual_holding: Where the accused inflicted repeated merciless blows on an unarmed victim after the victim was incapacitated, the accused acted in a cruel and unusual manner; benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC cannot be claimed.
verbatim_excerpt: When the accused continued to strike repeated blows on the deceased after he fell defenseless, he took undue advantage and acted in a cruel manner. Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC cannot be invoked.

title: Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa
bench: Justice Ashok Bhushan and Justice K.M. Joseph
legal_issues: Section 138 NI Act,Section 139 NI Act Presumption,Standard of Proof for Accused
procedural_context: Criminal appeal against conviction under S. 138 NI Act for cheque dishonour
actual_holding: Presumption under S. 139 can be rebutted on preponderance of probabilities. To rebut, accused is not required to step into witness box; he can rely on materials produced by complainant or cross-examination.
verbatim_excerpt: To rebut the presumption, it is open to the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defense.

title: Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI
bench: Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul and Justice M.M. Sundresh
procedural_context: Comprehensive Supreme Court guidelines on arrest and bail
actual_holding: Bail is the rule and jail is the exception. Arrest should not be made mechanically where offence is punishable with up to 7 years without complying with Section 41 and Section 41A CrPC.
verbatim_excerpt: Courts must not adopt a mechanical approach in denying bail. The investigating agency must strictly comply with Section 41 and 41A CrPC.

title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
bench: Justice Chandramauli Kumar Prasad and Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose
legal_issues: Section 41 CrPC,Section 41A CrPC Notice of Appearance,Section 498A IPC,Mandatory Safeguards Against Mechanical Arrest,Contempt of Court for Police Default
procedural_context: Special Leave Petition arising from rejection of anticipatory bail in Section 498A IPC matter
actual_holding: Arrest should not be made mechanically in offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Police officers must serve a notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC within two weeks from the date of institution of the case. Failure to comply with Section 41/41A CrPC renders police officers liable for departmental action and contempt of court. Magistrates authorizing detention without recording satisfaction also face disciplinary proceedings.
verbatim_excerpt: We believe that no arrest should be made only because the offence is non-bailable and cognizable... Notice of appearance in terms of Section 41A CrPC be served on the accused within two weeks from the date of institution of the case... Failure to comply with directions aforesaid shall apart from departmental action render police officers liable to be punished for contempt of court.

title: Md. Asfak Alam v. State of Jharkhand
bench: Justice S. Ravindra Bhat and Justice Aravind Kumar
legal_issues: Section 41A CrPC Compliance,Pre-Arrest Safeguards,Article 21 Personal Liberty
procedural_context: Appeal against High Court refusal of anticipatory bail in matrimonial prosecution
actual_holding: Reaffirmed the mandatory binding nature of Arnesh Kumar directions. All High Courts and State Police Chiefs must enforce strict adherence to Section 41A CrPC notices before any custodial arrest in offences carrying sentence of 7 years or less.
verbatim_excerpt: This Court in Arnesh Kumar emphasized that arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom and casts scars forever. The directions in Arnesh Kumar must be scrupulously enforced without exception.

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
bench: Justice Kuldip Singh and Justice Dr. A.S. Anand
legal_issues: Custodial Violence,Arrest Guidelines,Preparation of Arrest Memo,Articles 21 and 22
procedural_context: Public interest litigation concerning custodial deaths and institutional safeguards
actual_holding: Laid down 11 mandatory procedural requirements to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention, including contemporaneous arrest memo, right to inform next friend, and medical inspection.
verbatim_excerpt: Custodial violence, including torture and death in the lock-up, strikes a blow at the rule of law. The requirements laid down herein flow from Articles 21 and 22(1) of the Constitution and must be strictly followed.

title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
bench: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, Justice P.N. Bhagwati, Justice N.L. Untwalia, Justice R.S. Pathak, Justice O. Chinnappa Reddy
legal_issues: Section 438 CrPC,Anticipatory Bail Jurisdiction,Personal Liberty Article 21
procedural_context: Constitution Bench reference on principles governing grant of anticipatory bail
actual_holding: Section 438 CrPC confers wide discretionary power to protect innocent persons from harassment. The power must not be circumscribed by rigid judicially-created fetters or conditions not found in the statute.
verbatim_excerpt: The power conferred by Section 438 is of an extraordinary character, but extraordinary powers are given to meet extraordinary situations. The provisions of Section 438 must be read in the light of Article 21 of the Constitution.

title: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
bench: Chief Justice K.G. Balakrishnan, Justice P. Sathasivam, Justice J.M. Panchal
legal_issues: Section 139 NI Act,Reverse Onus Clause,Rebuttal by Preponderance of Probabilities
procedural_context: Three-Judge Bench reference resolving conflict on scope of Section 139 presumption
actual_holding: The presumption mandated by Section 139 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. However, the standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is only preponderance of probabilities, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.
verbatim_excerpt: The presumption that the cheque was issued in discharge of any debt or other liability is a presumption of law. The standard of proof evidently is that of preponderance of probabilities.
